title: Ouilets: Little Apps for Deciding Together
summary: A family of no-account, phone-first apps for deciding things together: what to watch, where to eat, and who is winning. Three apps, one monorepo, shipped to the web and to a native mobile host in about five weeks of evenings.

challenge.p: Picking a film with more than one person is a negotiation: endless scrolling, arguing over the shortlist, and forgetting which streaming services the household even pays for. Picking a restaurant is worse, because everyone says "I don't mind." And keeping score at the kitchen table always ends with someone disputing a number.
Each of these is a tiny product, which made the platform question the interesting one. The constraints I set for the whole family of apps:

ul: No accounts. A device token bound to a claimed name and a four-letter join code is the entire identity model.
Ephemeral by design: parties expire after seven days, and the app never plays video. It only decides.
Free-tier hosting only, so every design choice had to fit a Vercel Hobby, Render free and MongoDB Atlas M0 budget.
Build the second and third app without copying the first, and without turning a weekend project into a micro-frontend platform.

solution.p: One Bun workspaces monorepo with an app contract: each ouilet exports a small OuiApp object (base path, brand, root component), and the web shell lazy-loads it and sets the brand on the document. A micro-frontend-ready seam with no federation, recorded in the first ADR.

solution.alt: Oui! Let's... on iPhone: the launcher, a Watch Together lobby with party code and streaming services, a swipe card, a match, and the decided screen.

ul: A shared party engine that owns lobby, join codes, presence and phase state over one Socket.IO room per party, with a headless subpath so web and native share the same engine. A test walks the headless barrel and fails if anything but react, socket.io-client and the shared package leaks in.

Watch Together: swipe-to-match against the TMDB catalog, filtered to the services the group actually has. Lobby events use a load, pure-reducer, save loop with optimistic concurrency; swipes use a single atomic, idempotent update so five people swiping at once cannot cause a retry storm. Matches are re-verified live against streaming availability before they are announced.
Eat Together: Google Places text search with three-bucket preferences and hard quota caps so a busy night cannot run up a bill.
Keep Score: every entered score stays pending until another player approves it, and self-approval is rejected server-side.
Multi-brand theming from one stylesheet: the three brands differ by hue only, scoped by a data-brand attribute, with a parity test in CI.
A native host on Expo and React Native that runs Watch Together natively, opens the other ouilets in-app, and consumes design tokens generated from the same brand CSS.
A structure doctrine enforced by four custom gates in CI and pre-commit: hub-and-spoke layout, one component per file, import layers checked with dependency-cruiser, and brand parity.
Live at ouilets.com with three apps, six shared packages and one API, built in roughly five weeks across 293 commits.
1,058 tests across web, native and API, running on one CI job alongside the structure gates.
Native app built for both stores: the iOS build is processed in TestFlight and the Android release bundle is signed for the Play Console.
Runs at zero fixed cost. Monetisation is affiliate links only where a link already existed, plus a one-off Supporter purchase through Stripe, verified server-side.
Seven ADRs and thirteen design specs mean the next ouilet is one OuiApp export and a shell route, not a new repo.

title: GlobalJam: Remote Rehearsal for Bands
summary: A platform for bands split across cities and countries to rehearse together and come away with time-aligned, multi-track recordings. A React micro-frontend host, fourteen Go services and a native Rust audio bridge, shipped to production and then rebuilt to run at zero hosting cost.

challenge.p: The founding case is my own: a band with members in Auckland and Gainesville, Florida, about 13,000 km apart. Ensemble playing breaks down above roughly 25 ms of one-way latency, intercontinental round trips sit near 200 ms, and browsers add 20 to 100 ms of audio overhead on top. No amount of engineering makes that disappear.
So the product question became: what is honestly possible, and what is worth paying for?

ul: Audio has to leave the browser. Direct device access, Opus with forward error correction and an adaptive jitter buffer are a native problem.
Every musician needs a shared clock and a shared click, so that whatever they hear live, the recording lines up sample-accurately.
Peer-to-peer UDP fails behind many home and campus networks, so the audio path needs its own relay.
The first production footprint on Kubernetes cost low hundreds of dollars a month with zero users. The platform had to survive long enough to find them.

solution.alt: GlobalJam web app: sign in, the welcome walkthrough, the Audio Bridge setup step, the rooms list, inside a room waiting for bandmates, and session history.

ul: A native Audio Bridge in Rust: CPAL device I/O, Opus at 48 kHz in 20 ms frames with in-band FEC, UDP peer-to-peer transport, a 5 to 40 ms adaptive jitter buffer, dropout detection and a soft-knee master limiter. Signed and notarised macOS builds, with Windows and Linux builds from the same workflow.

Tempo-Lock: NTP-style clock sync over UDP to sub-millisecond offsets, a shared click at session tempo, and onset detection, so every stream is timestamped and sessions render as time-aligned 24-bit FLAC stems plus a click stem.
Two-plane audio: talk-back voice rides WebRTC with echo cancellation and noise suppression; performance audio never touches it.

Per-pair topology chosen from measured round-trip time: direct UDP under 25 ms, Tempo-Lock above it, and a TURN relay built into the bridge when UDP is blocked, with ephemeral HMAC credentials and peer attribution keyed on channel number rather than packet source.

A React 19 micro-frontend host on Rspack and Module Federation with ten feature plugins (rooms, sessions, bands, audio bridge, video, livestream and more), backed by fourteen Go services behind a routes-driven gateway with JWT, RBAC and a Redis-backed WebSocket hub.

Cost collapse without a rewrite: the thirteen Kubernetes deployments were composed into one Go binary through per-service build packages and moved to Render, Neon Postgres, Backblaze B2 and an Oracle Always Free VM for TURN. Every existing test still runs.
Twelve ADRs, a Stripe billing design, and a crew of 31 repo-scoped AI agents and 18 skills that executed implementation waves in parallel git worktrees.
Shipped to production at global-jams.com through v1.0.10 with a three-stage promotion pipeline (test, release candidate, production) on byte-identical images.
948 commits in six months, with 2,517 Go tests, 919 Rust tests and 3,444 frontend test cases, plus Playwright end-to-end coverage.
Monthly hosting cost went from low hundreds of dollars to zero with no feature loss.
The honest latency model reframed the product: sell remote rehearsal with every part captured as a stem, not fake real-time jamming. That is the MVP now being validated with outside bands.
